title: Gate-level Implementation and Resource Analysis of Lackadaisical Quantum Walk Search
authors: Amit Saha, Debanjan Kola, Nishanka Das, Amlan Chakrabarti
abstract: Lackadaisical quantum walks (LQW) extend discrete-time quantum walks (DTQW) by introducing weighted self-loops, enabling improved spatial-search performance through controlled localization of the walker. Although their theoretical properties and algorithmic advantages have been studied extensively, practical gate-level realizations suitable for execution on quantum hardware remain largely unexplored. This gap limits the assessment of lackadaisical quantum walk search under realistic architectural constraints, noise processes, and resource requirements. In this work, we present a gate-level implementation framework for lackadaisical quantum walk search. The proposed construction encodes the position and coin spaces into qubit registers, and realizes the walk dynamics through oracle, coin, and flip-flop shift operations. We validate the circuit by reproducing the expected search behavior for single and multiple marked vertices and by analyzing the effect of the self-loop weight on the success probability. We further evaluate the implementation under realistic noisy settings using superconducting hardware's noise models and apply noise-mitigation techniques to improve the measured search performance. Logical-resource analysis shows that, for grids ranging from $8\times8$ to $64\times64$, the algorithmic register increases from 9 to 15 qubits, while the transpiled gate count increases from $3.63\times10^{5}$ to $4.38\times10^{6}$ and the circuit depth from $2.13\times10^{5}$ to $2.56\times10^{6}$. Finally, fault-tolerant resource estimates based on a surface-code model using the Microsoft Quantum Resource Estimator demonstrate the substantial space-time trade-off associated with magic-state production.
summary: This paper provides a comprehensive gate-level implementation framework for Lackadaisical Quantum Walk search, bridging the gap between theory and hardware. The authors detail the circuit construction, validate its performance under noise, and rigorously analyze the required quantum resources using both logical and fault-tolerant estimates. This work establishes a practical roadmap for testing advanced quantum search algorithms on superconducting quantum hardware.
main_problem: The paper addresses the gap between the theoretical advantages of Lackadaisical Quantum Walks (LQW) and their practical, gate-level realization for execution on current quantum hardware.
main_result: They provide a complete, validated gate-level circuit construction for LQW search and perform detailed resource analyses, quantifying the required qubits and gate counts for scaling up to large grids.
method: The authors developed a gate-level framework by encoding the walk dynamics using oracle, coin, and flip-flop shift operations, validating the circuit under both ideal and realistic noisy superconducting hardware models.
model_or_system: The model is the Lackadaisical Quantum Walk (LQW) on a 2D grid, which extends standard quantum walks by incorporating weighted self-loops to enhance search localization. The implementation is mapped onto a qubit register structure suitable for superconducting quantum hardware.
key_observables: Search success probability, algorithmic register size (9 to 15 qubits), transpiled gate count ($3.63	imes10^{5}$ to $4.38	imes10^{6}$), and circuit depth.
important_parameters: Self-loop weight ($\ell$), grid size ($8	imes8$ to $64	imes64$), physical error rate ($p=10^{-3}$), and code distance for surface-code analysis.
main_assumptions: The physical resource analysis assumes a surface-code model and relies on the decomposability of multi-controlled gates into native one- and two-qubit gates.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the 1D and 2D walk structures, basic coin circuits, and the circuit components (increment/decrement) used for the position register.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the LQW model and its theoretical benefits, to presenting the explicit gate-level circuit construction, validating it under noise, and concluding with detailed logical and fault-tolerant physical resource estimations.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it translates an abstract quantum algorithm into concrete, resource-quantified circuit blueprints, which is the necessary step for experimental realization on near-term quantum processors.
